transcription.text: I'm here with Malcolm Fade from the Manly Radio Society, and we're at their amateur radio meeting.
Is this weekly or is it monthly?
It is weekly. One Wednesday a month we have our business meeting.
One Wednesday a month we have a lecture, which we've had tonight, from Gavin.
And the other two or three are just free-for-alls. We come along and talk and play radio.
Yeah, as you do in amateur radio clubs.
So tell us some of your gear. Take us around your shop here.
I can tell you about some of the newer things. I'll leave the older stuff to somebody more experienced than I.
We've got an HF set here from Yasu.
This is our main radio that we use for long-distance contact.
Above it we have an antenna rotator.
We have a Yagi on a tower outside, so we're able to talk around the world with that and direct the antenna in the right direction.
We've got here an ICOM radio, IC2820, which is a dual mode.
It's FM analog and FM voice, and digital voice as well.
A mode called D-Star, where the voice is encoded in digital form and transmitted and decoded at the other end.
The Manly Warringah Radio Society hosts repeaters up at Terry Hills, just not far from here.
There's 2m 70cm analog voice repeaters.
And also we have 2m 70cm D-Star repeaters.
Soon to have a 23cm D-Star.
And we also have an APCO 25 repeater as well on 70cm.
I'm sure the hands out there are all salivating and know exactly what you're talking about.
I'm sure they do.
We're in a good location here. We can service a lot of Sydney.
It's a very old and established club.
The earliest reference we can find to the club is back in the 1920s.
So it's quite a history.
Excellent. And it's still going. And you've got this place pretty much all to yourself now?
Almost. We rent the hall from the Girl Guides.
It's still used by various organisations and the Girl Guides, so we don't quite have completely free use of it.
But we've got our own little radio room here that's well stocked where we can have fun and play radio.
And some antennas outside as well.
Excellent. Well, you've got to have antennas.
What other stuff have you got?
Well, we have a few other older radios.
I will leave somebody else to talk about those.
But these are your main two bits of kit, right?
These are our main kit. This one?
This is fairly new. We only bought that last year.
There's a few other.
Any homemade bits of kit?
Anything homemade.
Very good question.
Because hands homemake everything, right?
Not everything, no.
The quality of radios that you can buy, it's not really worth it.
But we do modify, and a lot of us do homebrew, smaller things, smaller kits.
One of the gentlemen here, who unfortunately isn't here tonight, plays with Software Defined Radios.
He builds his own, which is fantastic.
But how can you compete with a transceiver like that, chrome-built? You really can't.
Software Defined Radios is the closest you can really get, where you can do everything in software.
It takes a smarter person than I to write demodulators and modulators for that.
And, Webb, this is your world map over here.
Yes, it's a dated one. That's our world map.
It includes the callsign prefixes for various countries around the world.
Here we can see ZL, my homeland, VK for Australia.
Here we can see the third letter of the prefix, 2 for New South Wales, 3 for Victoria, etc.
And where we were talking to before was OE.
OE, so somewhere in Austria?
I think that's either Austria or Slovenia. It's a little hard to tell on the map.
And is English the default?
English is the default.
Yes, it is.
Yes, it is.
But when we arrived before, one of the gentlemen from Canada, that's a member here, he was talking to a guy in France in French.
Oh, OK.
So, once you've made a contact, you speak another language, it's all good.
Or is that frowned upon?
I don't think it's frowned upon.
Because people want to listen in?
Not really.
No? OK.
It's OK.
Is there a lot of idiots on it?
You know, like on CB radio, the idiots took over and they own that.
Does Ham get a lot of...
No, it's fairly well controlled.
The reason for that is because it is licensed, and the ACMA, who is the regulatory body in Australia,
and the parallel bodies in other countries are quite strict about the use of the radio spectrum.
And you'll get knocks on your door if you do bad things.
So how does the antenna rotator work?
Well, there is a motor up the tower, connected to a shaft, and that shaft is connected to the antenna.
If I push the button, it rotates the antenna around the horizontal axis,
and will point to whatever point on the compass that you wish it to.
There is a potentiometer attached to the shaft up there, and that's what gives the feedback to the needle.
Right.
Can you set it to automatically do sweeps and then stop when it finds a particular signal?
Not really.
What you can do, if this one doesn't do it, is you can rotate the needle,
and then the antenna will just follow it in its own time.
We've found some homebrew stuff by the looks of it.
They're all Morse keys by the looks of it.
These are all homebrew Morse keys.
There's another one down here.
Homebrew Morse.
It's a cute one made from PCB.
Nice.
And that looks like a bought one.
It certainly is.
Do you do much Morse?
Here, the guys are into Morse.
The great thing about an amateur radio club is different people are into different things.
I enjoy it for the tech, and I enjoy radio a little bit as well.
Some guys really love the HF and making long-range contact.
Some people like APRS, packet radio.
We have an APRS digipeter up here,
which receives APRS packets from the northern end of the northern beaches,
up to Wyong in that direction.
That digipetes up to an iGate, which receives RF
and pushes the APRS into the global APRS network.
Other people enjoy HF for four-wheel driving and keeping in contact with friends.
Some people like building kits.
There's all sorts of things.
We also help with the annual JOTA, Jamboree on the Air,
which is a scouting event.
It was a big quite a few decades or two back.
Is it still going?
It's still very active.
Just a few weeks ago was when the event was,
and we had a few hundred scouts and guides and cubs.
Fantastic.
Doing all amateur radio.
Do you still do fox hunts?
Fox hunts?
Yep.
This was made especially for scouts.
A fox hunt antenna.
Oh, that's brilliant.
It's made out of tape measures.
It's absolutely fantastic.
That is great.
This is for two meters.
A little Yagi.
It's the matching stub here.
If you walk into a tree.
They are a metal blade.
It just bends.
That's fantastic.
I love it.
Just don't take an eye out.
That's brilliant.
It works very well.
They do.
Some of the kids made one each.
Right.
As a project.
Fantastic.
Show us your T-shirt.
A few years ago,
I was lucky enough to go to a maker fair in Austin, Texas.
Oh, I'm jealous.
Arc Attack was one of the primo things to see.
The thing is to see a guy in a cage.
They had the big cage.
They didn't have the cage when I was there,
but they did have the two Tesla coils.
The two Tesla coils.
This is a schematic, I guess, of the driver.
One of the original ones.
Awesome.
Thanks, Malcolm.
How much is a rig like this?
How much is it worth?
When you're about $4,000,
this is now probably 15-year-old technology.
We've had this radio for probably 12 years.
On the second-hand market now,
maybe $2,000.
Are there any advantages in the newer models?
Has it got any newer capability?
Or is old gear like this sufficient?
The old gear is sufficient to get you on air,
but there's no comparison.
It's like motor cars, I guess.
You could still drive to work in a Morris Minor
if you wanted to,
but you know what I'm trying to say.
Are you talking about tuner sensitivity?
The receivers are a lot more selective.
The filters are better.
This radio's got basically two receivers in it.
They can receive on two different parts of the band.
You can hit buttons and change from one VFO to the other,
which means that you can reverse them.
You can decide which one you want to transmit on
by just pressing the button.
You see that one's gone red there.
Now it's red here, so I'm transmitting on this one.
It's a lot more versatile,
and that's only been happening in radios
for probably, hard to say, 15 or 20 years.
Right.
Are there a lot of hands using
softly defined radio VFOs?
Yeah, it's becoming more and more popular.
I haven't had a lot to do with that,
but what I have done is it hasn't got the feel
of actually tuning like this.
But could you have a softly defined radio
with the nice knobs on the front with the readout?
That's coming too.
Right.
Yeah, and the ones that I've used
that put receivers in nice and quiet
seem to work really well,
but I haven't had enough experience
to really comment on how they compare
with these units.
But yeah, I think you'll probably find
that in another 10 years
they'll probably all be softly defined.
Right.
I'm just trying to,
it's hard to sort of tune around
and find a Morse code signal and talk
at the same time.
Okay, that was Gene in Kirov.
He repeated his location, so yeah.
Kirov somewhere in Russia.
In Russia, excellent.
So what's the advantage of this side-by-side key?
Okay, I'll turn the key off
so I'm not transmitting at all.
Yep.
I'll explain that to you.
What happens is one size does this,
one size does that.
So instead of having a conventional key
like this, where depending on how long
you hold the button down,
you'd have to time it.
This is timed by electronic circuitry
within the radio.
One size does this.
You can rest your arm on the bench
and it's just a matter of you working out
your timing between your fingers.
Right.
And generally, I'd say if you're handy
with one of these,
everyone usually does their exam
with one of these.
One of those, right.
And to transform to one of these,
probably a weekend of practice.
Right, so that one's more accurate though?
Oh yeah.
Faster, cleaner, better.
Right.
I think an analogy that one of the guys
here uses is that a builder could build
a house using an egg beater drill,
but he chooses not to.
He uses an electric drill.
Yep.
Right, and that's what we do nowadays
is we use an electronic key.
Right, and the radio actually supports
that really.
Has it built in?
Yeah.
A lot of radios these days actually
have memories in there too,
so you can type your call sign
into the radio,
and you can put all your commonly sent stuff,
your name, your location, your call sign,
and when you're talking to someone,
if you just hit memory number whatever,
it'll send something like,
hello, my name's Russ,
I'm in Sydney, Australia,
and the weather's fine.
That almost takes the fun out of it,
doesn't it?
Yeah, I don't use that sort of thing very much.
Well, you can almost get to a point
where you can hook up a keyboard
and type it in.
Oh, people do that.
Right.
That is the step up after.
Right.
But for those of us that are purists,
you can actually transmit faster
with one of these than on a keyboard.
Right, okay.
How many words per minute?
Look, it depends how much time you put into it,
but certainly 40 is not out of the question.
Right, okay.
There are plenty of guys that do that sort of speed.
Right.
And even faster,
but it gets to the stage
where it starts to fall to pieces
if you don't time it perfectly.
Right.
It's like handwriting.
If it's nice and clean and done properly,
it's easy to read.
Right.
So you'd class yourself as a purist,
so you use the traditional Morse key.
Is there anything else?
Would you frown upon others
who use the keyboard or automated?
No, no, no, no.
There's no elitist thing happening?
No, no, no.
If people want to use a keyboard and a computer,
that's fine,
but I think you'd find that in most cases
this is still a more popular key than a keyboard.
Right.
In contests, memory keying has become more and more popular.
There are programs that will actually number the contacts you have
and work out points at the end of the competition.
Of course, depending on the areas you talk to
and the number of contacts that you have
over the course of a weekend,
they build up points,
and that's done with a computer keyboard.
But just for having a contact on Morse
and having just a chin wave,
the paddle key is probably the way to go.
Fantastic.
So we just spoke to someone from Russia.
Here I am in Russia.
On what, 14.01 MHz?
Yeah, 14.012 or thereabouts.
I've moved the dial a little bit,
but somewhere about there, yeah.
Okay.
Is that common for this time of night?
Would you be able to get them only at night,
during the day, atmospheric?
No.
Yeah, it does open up at different times of the day,
and what happens is if you're on every day,
you get into a pattern of knowing
what's going to happen tomorrow
or having a pretty fair idea,
but it changes.
This band is particularly good at afternoons,
early in the mornings,
and you follow your dark path.
How it works is that where the sun is in the sky,
it tends to be a little bit flat.
So we're ahead of the rest of the world with the sun,
so in the morning you work the short path to Europe.
I used to get on at five or six in the morning,
and as the sun's rising here,
it's still dark in Europe,
and that's a very good path.
Some of the Russian areas,
I don't know where he was actually,
I've looked it up on the Atlas,
it was Kirov,
but some of the Russia wraps around,
halfway around the world,
and part of Russia is due north of Australia,
and that's a dark path.
So we've probably got him on the dark path.
So you'd be using a directional antenna?
Yeah, absolutely.
You don't always use a directional antenna?
Yeah, it's better if you can.
It depends on how much room you've got to put it up,
and of course your budget.
It's a hobby for people.
Some people can only afford a length of wire.
Other people can afford a very expensive tower antenna.
But we've got a 6mm up there.
What's the bandwidth for that?
It does 20 metres, 15 and 10.
The bandwidth depends on where you tune it to,
but with the tuners that are in these radios,
you can do the whole band,
within three bands.
And it works pretty well.
It's a great piece of kit.
Fantastic.
Are there any interference from sunspots
and high solar activity?
Every 12 years, right?
Yeah, 11 years or whatever it is.
11 years you get a solar peak,
and it's been flat now for years,
but it's been very, very flat.
Almost zero sunspots, hasn't it?
Must be good times for them.
It's starting to get better now,
and I'm just thinking that I'll have to put
my Yagi antenna up at home again.
I've had it down for 12 months while I serviced it,
so I'll have to get back into it.
But it's only in the last year or so
that things have been picking up.
So we're up on pretty much a hill here at the moment,
aren't we?
Terry Hills.
This is a good location for radio.
It's a little bit out of the CBD.
It's a little bit quiet.
I was going to say,
what about the urban...
The urban sprawl.
What have cell towers done to the ham?
Well, not so much cell towers.
Plasma TVs are a killer.
Plasma TVs?
Yeah.
But here where we are,
we're sort of on the edge of the bush.
We've got a few neighbours across the road,
but they're far enough away that it's...
For being in Sydney, it's a very quiet location.
Yeah, because Sydney's quite a big suburban sprawl.
Yeah.
And we're on sort of the northeastern edge of it.
And you can pretty much contact any point on the road?
Given the right conditions.
Oh, yeah.
We can certainly get anywhere.
But you just have to pick your band
and be a little bit lucky.
Fantastic.
Now, my own part of the hobby,
I like working 80 metres, which is 3.5 metres.
And it's a real challenge to work as many times as you can
on those lower frequencies.
Like on 20, we just did it there.
We got a big man on the first call.
Easy.
Not so easy on 3.5 metres to get into Russia.
But it does happen.
I was reading something the other night
about this huge Russian transceiver in the 60s
that it would...
The woodpecker.
The woodpecker, that's it.
Is that...
Is that quite a slow operation?
Not as much, no.
Like, that sort of...
I don't know how long ago.
I certainly was going in the late 70s and early 80s.
I don't know exactly how long it's been on there.
But people used to say it was a Russian
over-the-horizon radar system.
I've seen it.
It's amazing.
I've seen photos of it.
It's huge.
It's round a metre tall or something.
And it used to chirp right across the band.
It drove us nuts.
It drove us nuts for years and years and years.
You worked around it.
It was just one of those things.
You couldn't do anything about it.
You get some of the hands with actually
some sort of...
They sort of reverse-engineered the data
that was coming out,
and then retransmitted it to force them
to change their algorithms and move bands.
May well have done if I didn't hear that.
It's a great, great hobby.
Nah, it's a very interesting hobby.
There's all sorts of fabulous digital modes
you can hook up to your computer
and transmit.
Slow-scan television.
All sorts of weird and wonderful things.
And the beautiful thing about technology nowadays,
when I first got into the hobby in the 70s
to send slow-scan television,
one of the guys in this club
actually bought the equipment to do it.
It cost him about $2,000 in the late 70s.
Now, if you've got a laptop computer
or even a desktop,
the software is freeware.
Fantastic.
It costs you a couple of resistors,
a length of cable with a microphone plug on it.
So for $10 worth of parts,
you're doing slow-scan TV.
Fantastic.
So are there many young guys getting into it in Sydney?
Yeah.
Since they dropped the Morse code requirement
and brought in what we call a foundation licence,
it's lifted the interest rate
in young people a hell of a lot,
and we've had probably a dozen young members
join in the last 12 months, two years.
Fantastic. What age bracket are we talking?
Twenties to thirties,
and we've had a couple of teenagers.
Teenagers? Fantastic.
That's one of those things.
But the Morse code requirement
was always one that required a big commitment.
How long did it take to get proficient enough
to actually pass?
I did it in three months,
practicing every day,
but I saw it as a challenge.
The first time I saw it demonstrated,
I thought I'd never do it,
so I put my mind to it,
and I did with about 20 or 30 minutes practice every day
in three months I had the ticket.
All right, Ross, tell us about some of the gear you've got.
This is an old Kenwood TS-520
from the early or mid-1970s.
It's a transistorised receiver,
but the output stage is valves.
It's got two finals and a 12BY7A driver tube,
about 100 watts output,
and a beautiful, beautiful old piece of kit.
Nice, quiet receiver.
To actually use this radio on a receive,
it's every bit as good as this later piece of kit.
Really?
Not quite as selective.
Hasn't got the features of dual VFOs
and that sort of thing,
but as far as listening to someone talking
or having a Morse code QSR,
lovely piece of kit to use.
Nice old radio.
How much would they cost on eBay these days
if you can still find them?
Oh, you can still find them.
In fact, I looked at one yesterday.
Hard to say.
It depends if it comes with the microphones alone.
The desktop microphone's probably worth $100 these days,
but the radio itself, about $300.
So you can buy a radio for $300,
a handheld microphone for probably $20,
or a desktop for another $100.
Put yourself a piece of wire in the air
and you'd be on air if you had a ticket.
If you've just got a new ticket
and you want to spend $500,
you can get on air very reliably for $500 easy.
Terrific.
And as we get a bit newer,
this is a Yasi piece of kit.
It belongs to one of the members.
This is from probably about,
what would that be?
1980 or thereabouts?
1980 vintage.
A little bit later than that Kenwood 520 we just looked at.
That's about 1980.
A few more features.
A bit fancier radio.
And what else can I show you?
Oh, we've got tuners.
Ventron tuner.
Another tuner up here.
We've got all sorts of bits and pieces
that the guys fiddle with.
Oscilloscopes.
Then we get into D-Staff.
Are you into homemade stuff?
I am not.
I'd rather operate than build,
but some of the guys do.
But the thing is,
the homemade stuff tends to be hobby transmitters
for one frequency.
It's very difficult.
It's not difficult.
You can do it.
But the thing is,
this stuff spoils you.
Yeah.
You know?
It's a bit like,
I suppose people out there can build their own motor car
or they can drive their whole Commodore.
It's one of those things.
Exactly.
So you mainly use the Yazoo down here?
Yeah, that's our club radio.
We bought that about 12 odd years ago.
And then shortly after that,
a gentleman donated this Yazoo FG-767,
which is a few years older than that.
But that's another nice, really nice radio.
That's from probably 20 years ago.
It's a great hobby.
It's a great hobby.
And this is a great club.
Excellent.
Thanks, Russ.
Okay.
Now there's a guy calling SIG here.
UA4NU is a Russian,
so we're going to give him a blast, okay?
Alright, so we're talking to Russian.
Yeah.
Hello.
Got him on the first call.
Nice work.
Hello.
His name is Gene and he's in Kirov.
Kirov?
Kirov, I think.
I think you're right.
Yeah.
And they're testing a VHF 2MHz EQ.
No, no, no.
Yes.
This is Victor Kirov 2, Mexico, Boston,
calling CQN, standing by.
Oscar Echo 5, Lima X-ray Papa.
This is Victor Kirov 2, Mexico, Boston.
Good evening to you.
The name this end is Greg Golf, Romeo Echo Golf.
You're 5 and 9 into Sydney, Australia.
Oscar Echo 5, Lima X-ray Papa.
This is Victor Kirov 2, Mexico, Boston.
Big pile up, Victor Kirov 3, Kirov Romeo.
I was trying to call, but I wasn't able to reach you,
and I hope I'm on the frequency.
I'm happy to listen to you, Greg.
Back to you.
Victor Kirov 3, OE5LXP, over.
Yeah, Oscar Echo 5, Lima X-ray Papa.
Victor Kirov 2, my brother.
Yeah, thanks for calling, Hans.
Nice to make the contact.
We just sort of, this is a radio club station in Sydney,
so we've just actually been doing a little bit
of a demonstration here for a video,
and we thought we'd actually put out a couple of calls
on 10 metres, seeing there's so much action,
but thank you very much for coming back to the call,
and look to catch up with you another day, Hans.
Thanks for the call.
Oscar Echo 5, Lima X-ray Papa.
